transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jules (Redwood Solutions), Maya (Ellipsia Eng Manager), Priya (Ellipsia SRE), Derek (Ellipsia Platform), Olivia (Ellipsia Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Ellipsia is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for inference. Key concerns: multi-region failover, graceful degradation (partial result vs retry), data residency and KMS, SLAs and runbooks, cost impact of hot-standby vs traffic-splitting. Next steps: send security artifacts, sizing spreadsheet, schedule pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for making time, we wanted to run through your outage mitigation and degradation approach and how Redwood can fit in, um, real quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: maya here, eng manager for the conversational payments team, i'm joined by priya our sre and derek who owns platform.
[00:13] Priya: hey.
[00:14] Derek: hey all.
[00:15] Alex: great — i'm alex, i'm the account lead, samir's our se and jules helps on rollout and ops.
[00:20] Samir (Redwood SE): hi all. quick note: i'll use "redwood hosted" or "redwood dedicated" in the call; sometimes the transcription flips names so sorry in advance.
[00:29] Maya: that's fine. Our ask: we need a plan for when a region becomes degraded — we run payment verification, so latency spikes cause timeouts and user drop-off. we're exploring hosted for speed of dev, dedicated for predictability, or private for compliance.
[00:43] Samir: totally. can you walk me through current traffic patterns, p95/p99 numbers, and where timeouts surface?
[00:50] Maya: baseline p95 for our inference calls is ~220ms, p99 is 1.2s during peak; we have bursts up to 3x for promo windows. most errors are client-side timeouts at 2s, and we see a lot of retries which amplifies load.
[01:05] Priya: and our SLO is 99.9% success for auth flows, latency budget 500ms for the majority of calls, but we accept degradation for low-risk intents.
[01:15] Samir: ok so two axes: capacity and graceful degradation. Redwood's routing supports policy-based region steering and automatic fallback to model variants (e.g., smaller / quantized) when latency or capacity thresholds are hit. we can also do prefix or KV cache to reduce token cost.
[01:34] Derek: curious — how does the fallback work practically? do you run hot-standby in another region or is it cold spin up?
[01:41] Samir: depends on the deployment mode. hosted has multi-region replicas we can route to, but cold spinups take longer. dedicated gives you pinned capacity in chosen regions — so predictable throughput and faster failover, but higher cost. private can be tuned for on-prem hot pairs if you need strict residency.
[01:56] Maya: cost is a big constraint. hot-standby everywhere is probably too expensive. what about partial degradation — like returning a cached or shorter completion rather than full failure?
[02:06] Jules (Redwood): we've seen teams use a graded degradation policy: 1) prefer same-region full model; 2) fallback to a smaller model in-region; 3) try cross-region reduced model with soft timeout; 4) return partial structured response or cached inference. that reduces retry storms and keeps downstream systems stable.
[02:24] Priya: ok, and is that automatic? who defines the thresholds?
[02:29] Samir: thresholds are policy driven — you define latency thresholds and capacity headroom. Redwood's control plane can automatically switch routes when p95 exceeds X or error rate hits Y. you can also set canary percentages for traffic shifting and have an automatic rollback window.
[02:44] Olivia (Security): questions on encryption and keys — if you do cross-region failover, how do you ensure KMS keys and audit logs remain compliant? we have rules that keys must remain in EU for EU traffic.
[02:55] Alex: good call. for Redwood Hosted we support region-scoped KMS and customer-managed keys; audit logs are forwarded to your SIEM via secure endpoints. for private deployments you retain full KMS control inside your VPC. we'll send the SOC2 and KMS integration docs after the call.
[03:12] Maya: another nuance: our fraud model needs deterministic outputs for some intents — switching to a quantized or smaller model changes behavior and could increase false positives. how do teams handle quality regressions during fallback?
[03:25] Samir: great point. we recommend a canary with a subset of traffic and eval metrics for intent drift — Redwood Optimize can run offline evals and flag regressions against your golden prompts. for high-risk intents you can pin to an in-region model and only fallback for low-risk intents.
[03:40] Derek: we also want to understand SLA commitments. what latency SLAs and availability do you offer for hosted vs dedicated?
[03:47] Alex: hosted has a best-effort SLA, production tiers get higher SLOs; Dedicated includes an SLA with uptime targets and latency percentiles in the contract. i can't quote numbers off the top of my head here, i'll attach the SLA terms to the post-call package.
[03:58] Priya: can we get an SLA that covers regional failover window? that's what we need for runbook metrics.
[04:04] Jules: yes, dedicated contracts include defined failover windows and response times for regional issues; we can map that to your runbook metrics (mttr, mttd).
[04:12] Maya: about traffic shaping — could we send low-risk traffic to cheaper quantized paths proactively, not just as a fallback?
[04:19] Samir: absolutely — that's routing by intent/route. you can tag routes and define cost-performance tiers: high-fidelity models for high-risk intents, quantized for standard responses. this is often the biggest unit-cost lever.
[04:30] Priya: any gotchas with KV cache and session affinity in multi-region? we learned the hard way with sticky sessions and cache invalidation.
[04:38] Samir: yes, session-affinity complicates multi-region cache. we recommend prefix caching and global cache keys with TTLs; for strict affinity you can favor region-local caches and accept slightly higher misses during failover.
[04:50] Olivia: audit and legal — will cross-region fallback create unexpected data egress? our lawyers will flag that.
[04:56] Alex: you can scope failovers to approved regions only; for EU traffic we can prevent cross-border fallback. we document data flows and provide a data residency matrix.
[05:06] Maya: what about chaos testing — can we run simulated outages to validate our runbook?
[05:10] Jules: yes, we support a chaos sim plan. teams run scheduled chaos tests against dedicated stacks or private deployments; we can help design experiments: region flaps, injected latency, and model degradation, then measure fallback path correctness.
[05:23] Derek: how fast is recovery typically? if we see region loss, how quickly does traffic move to the next target?
[05:29] Samir: with pre-warmed dedicated capacity, failover can be seconds to tens of seconds. hosted warm replicas are often tens of seconds to a few minutes depending on provisioning. private hot-pair can be seconds. exact numbers depend on your config and traffic shaping.
[05:42] Maya: okay, given our peak volumes during promos, i think dedicated in primary region + smaller dedicated pool in secondary is our conservative option. but cost is a blocker. can you model cost tradeoffs?
[05:53] Alex: yes — Samir will share a pilot sizing and pricing worksheet. we can model a hybrid: dedicated primary, hosted or shared dedicated for secondary with traffic caps to control cost.
[06:03] Priya: on instrumentation — what telemetry do we get? token-level latency, per-route error breakdown, per-model perf?
[06:10] Samir: you get per-route, per-model metrics, token spend breakdowns, traces and request IDs to link to your APM. we also support exporting metrics to Prometheus/Grafana and sending traces to lightstep/jaeger.
[06:22] Maya: good. one more operational question — in a regional outage we want to prioritize auth flows over low-risk chat. can we set priorities in the routing policy?
[06:30] Jules: yes, we support weighted priorities and preemption rules. you can rate-limit low-priority routes automatically and reserve capacity for P0 routes.
[06:38] Derek: for the pilot, we'd like to test a degrade strategy: step down model size in-region, then cross-region failover, and finally partial cached response. can Redwood orchestrate that chain?
[06:49] Samir: yes, we can define ordered fallbacks and set triggers. we'll surface observability events for each step so you can validate correctness in the runbook.
[06:58] Maya: ok, final non-technical: what's required from our side to start a pilot?
[07:03] Alex: ideally: 1) traffic profile (sample traces), 2) list of high vs low risk intents, 3) compliance constraints (regions + KMS), 4) a contact for deployment access. we'll take that and propose pilot config.
[07:16] Maya: we'll get that to you.
[07:18] Priya: question: does Redwood's platform throttle retries to prevent thundering herd during failover?
[07:23] Samir: yes, we have circuit breakers and client-side backoff recommendations; we can also implement server-side throttling for flood protection.
[07:31] Olivia: one last on logs — are audit trails tamper-evident? our auditors will ask for retention windows and proof of non-modification.
[07:39] Jules: audit logs are immutable when forwarded to customer-controlled storage; we also provide signed-event records for hosted flows. we'll include details in the security bundle.
[07:48] Maya: thanks, this was helpful. can we recap next steps?
[07:52] Alex: sure — recap: Alex send SOC2, KMS, and audit artifacts; Samir send pilot sizing and pricing worksheet; Jules send runbook template and chaos test checklist; Maya to provide traffic profile and intent list and confirm pilot date week of Nov 15.
[08:10] Maya: yep that works.
[08:12] Priya: thanks everyone.
[08:13] Derek: thanks.
[08:14] Alex: thanks all. we'll follow up by email with the package.

End of transcript.
